title: With the offering, to the offering
hookLine: the Purusha Sukta's last verse: the world begins as an offering, and giving is the first dharma
carry: yajna: the world began as an offering

cards: A jar on a kitchen counter, with a cloth over the top. Inside, a sour, bubbling paste: a sourdough starter. You make today's bread with a piece of yesterday's.
You feed the starter, take some for the loaf, and keep the rest going for next time. Every loaf comes from the one before.
Ask where the first starter came from, and the chain runs back further than anyone in the kitchen can see. The Purusha Sukta ends on a loop like that: its last two verses, and the first dharmas.

teach.h: SEVEN STICKS, THREE TIMES SEVEN FUEL.
teach.b: Verse fifteen gives the measurements of the great offering.

Seven sticks were laid around its fire, and three times seven were made its fuel, when the gods, spreading out the offering, bound the Purusha as what was offered. Then verse sixteen, the hymn's last.

teach.h: WITH THE OFFERING, TO THE OFFERING.
teach.b: With the offering, the gods offered to the offering. It loops back on itself: the offering is the means, the one who receives, and the act, all at once. Then: tani dharmani prathamany asan.
These were the first dharmas: the first right ways of things, set down by that offering. Here's the teaching, plainly. In this hymn the world doesn't start with a builder or a rulebook.
It starts as yajna, an offering, and giving is the first dharma. Hindu life keeps that loop going at the table.
The Bhagavad Gita picks it up: those who eat what remains of the offering are freed, it says, and those who cook only for themselves eat wrong.
And many Hindus say a Gita verse before meals, brahmarpanam: the offering is Brahman, what's poured is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire that is Brahman.

Giver, gift and fire, all one, the same loop as the hymn's last line. That's why a plate goes before God first, and comes back as prasad. Many teachers read it as a way to live: nothing is simply taken.

how: The Purusha Sukta is recited in Hindu worship and Vedic chanting. At home, many Hindus offer food to God before eating and receive it back as prasad, some saying Bhagavad Gita 4.24, brahmarpanam, before the meal.

games.why: yajnena yajnam ayajanta devah: with the offering, the gods offered to the offering. these were the first dharmas.

practice: Picture your next meal set in front of you, and don't start yet. Bring to mind where it came from: the soil, the rain, the hands that grew it, the one who cooked it.

If you pray, offer it first, as many Hindus do, with the Gita's brahmarpanam or in your own words, then take it back as something given. If you don't pray, simply pause and say thank you before the first bite.
When the real meal comes, do it for real.

wordCard.voice: The Purusha Sukta. It ends: with the offering, the gods offered to the offering, and these were the first dharmas.

orig.note: Sanskrit: right order, duty, the way things should go. In Rig Veda 10.90.16 the first dharmas are set by the great offering.

carryVoice: Your line: yajna, the world began as an offering. With the offering, they offered to the offering. Tomorrow: who first heard the Gayatri?

sources.ref: Rig Veda 10.90.15 (seven were the enclosing sticks, three times seven the fuel sticks, when the gods, spreading the offering, bound the Purusha as the offering)
Rig Veda 10.90.16 (these were the first dharmas; those great ones reached the high heaven where the ancient Sadhyas, the gods, are)
Bhagavad Gita 3.13 (those who eat what remains of the offering are freed; those who cook only for themselves eat wrong)
Bhagavad Gita 4.24 (the offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman)
